title: What are the primes in each of these eleven numbers?
description: Eleven numbers are each split into two factors, and every factor that is not prime is split again. The primes of each number are joined into one row and checked by multiplying back.
teaching_notes: One idea: split a number into two factors, keep splitting until only primes are left, then join the primes. Watch for students who stop while a composite factor such as four or eight is still in the row.

video_script.why: The child writes eleven numbers as a multiplication of primes, using the way of the book's example of seventy two.
video_script.substitution: the book's own eleven numbers, each split first into two factors
video_script.anchor: the eleven numbers of the book on the board, each with its small tree of factors ending in primes
video_script.payoff_line: Every one of the eleven numbers is now a row of primes only

final_answer.spoken: every one of the eleven numbers is now a row of primes only

video_script.design: The eleven numbers stand in a grid on the board. Each is split into two factors, the factors are split again, and the primes are joined into one row and checked.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the eleven numbers 64, 104, 105, 243, 320, 141, 1728, 729, 1024, 1331 and 1000 stand in a grid with a question mark

marks.book: the title card From your book appears
marks.nums: the eleven numbers appear one by one in a grid
marks.ask: a question mark appears beside the grid

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about prime factorisation.
<bookmark mark='nums'/>It gives eleven numbers, and the biggest is one thousand seven hundred and twenty eight.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Can we write each of them as a multiplication of primes only?

beats.on_screen: the grid of numbers stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a small tree: a number splits into two factors; a prime is circled and stays; a factor that is not prime splits again

marks.way: a small tree appears with a number splitting into two factors
marks.stay: a prime is circled in gold, and a factor that is not prime splits again

narration: <bookmark mark='way'/>We use the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='stay'/>A prime cannot be broken further, so it stays. Any other factor is split again.

marks.given: the eleven numbers are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, eleven numbers to write as a multiplication of primes.

beats.on_screen: To find: the prime factorisation of each number
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the prime factorisation of each number.

marks.split: each number splits into two factors, one number after another
marks.board: all eleven splits stay on the board

narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step one, split each number into two factors. For example, sixty four is eight times eight, and one thousand is ten times one hundred.
<bookmark mark='board'/>The board shows the split of every number.

marks.again: each factor that is not prime splits again, down to circled primes
marks.stay: 13, 47, 3, 5 and 11 stay and are circled in gold

narration: <bookmark mark='again'/>Step two, split every factor that is not prime. Eight becomes two times two times two, and twenty one becomes three times seven.
<bookmark mark='stay'/>Primes such as thirteen and forty seven stay as they are.

marks.join: the primes of each number slide together into one line, number by number

beats.colours: 2s in teal, 3s in amber, other primes in gold
narration: <bookmark mark='join'/>Step three, join the primes of each number into one line. Multiplying in any order gives the same number, so the order does not matter.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check by multiplying back: 3 × 5 = 15 and 15 × 7 = 105; 11 × 11 = 121 and 121 × 11 = 1331; six 2s make 64 and three 3s make 27, then 64 × 27 = 1728

marks.big: six 2s turn into 64 and three 3s turn into 27

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step four, check by multiplying back. Three times five times seven is one hundred and five.
<bookmark mark='eleven'/>Eleven times eleven is one hundred and twenty one. That times eleven is one thousand three hundred and thirty one.
<bookmark mark='big'/>Six twos make sixty four, and three threes make twenty seven.
<bookmark mark='big2'/>Sixty four times twenty seven is one thousand seven hundred and twenty eight.

marks.ans: the eleven rows are boxed in green
marks.twos: the rows of 64 and 1024 light up
marks.threes: the rows of 243 and 729 light up
marks.mixed: the rows of 1331 and 104 light up
marks.mixed2: the rows of 105 and 141 light up
marks.big: the rows of 320 and 1000 light up

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Every one of the eleven numbers is now a row of primes only.
<bookmark mark='twos'/>Sixty four is six twos multiplied, and one thousand and twenty four is ten twos.
<bookmark mark='threes'/>Two hundred and forty three is five threes, and seven hundred and twenty nine is six threes.
<bookmark mark='mixed'/>One thousand three hundred and thirty one is three elevens. One hundred and four is three twos and thirteen.
<bookmark mark='mixed2'/>One hundred and five is three, five and seven. One hundred and forty one is three and forty seven.
<bookmark mark='big'/>Three hundred and twenty is six twos and one five. One thousand is three twos and three fives.
<bookmark mark='last'/>One thousand seven hundred and twenty eight is six twos and three threes.
